title: Πρὸ πυλάων
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: The Trojans are inside the walls, cooling off like fawns, while the Achaeans come up to the wall; only Hector is left outside, held by his fate before the Scaean Gates. Apollo, who has been luring Achilles away from the city, now speaks in his own person: Achilles has been chasing a god, and cannot kill him. Achilles answers angrily that the god has cheated him of glory and saved the Trojans, and that he would take vengeance if he could, and then he runs for the city like a racehorse. Priam sees him coming, shining like the evil-bringing Dog Star, and from the wall begs Hector to come inside: he names his lost sons, pictures his own death and the dogs at his doors, and tears his grey hair. Hecuba, her robe opened, holds out the breast that nursed him and begs him to keep the enemy off from behind the wall.

sentences.t:
ὣς οἳ μὲν κατὰ ἄστυ πεφυζότες ἠΰτε νεβροὶ
ἱδρῶ ἀπεψύχοντο πίον τ’ ἀκέοντό τε δίψαν
κεκλιμένοι καλῇσιν ἐπάλξεσιν·
sentences.tr:
hōs hoi men kata asty pephyzotes ēÿte nebroi
hidrō apepsychonto pion t’ akeonto te dipsan
keklimenoi kalēisin epalxesin·
sentences.i: So they, in flight through the town like fawns, cooled the sweat off themselves, and drank, and eased their thirst, leaning on the fine battlements;
sentences.n: Book 22 opens inside the walls of Troy: the Trojans who fled at the end of Book 21 are catching their breath, while outside the gates the Achaeans advance. ὣς οἳ μέν ‘so they, for their part’ looks back to the Trojans’ rush into the city, and its μέν is answered by αὐτὰρ Ἀχαιοί in the next unit. πεφυζότες is the perfect participle of a verb for panic flight (from φύζα), ‘put to flight’; ἠΰτε νεβροί ‘like fawns’. ἱδρῶ is the accusative of ἱδρώς ‘sweat’, and ἀπεψύχοντο the imperfect of ἀποψύχω ‘cool off’. πίον is an unaugmented aorist of πίνω ‘drink’, and ἀκέοντο the imperfect of ἀκέομαι ‘heal, mend’: they were curing their thirst. κεκλιμένοι is the perfect participle of κλίνω, ‘leaning’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ἀχαιοὶ
τείχεος ἆσσον ἴσαν σάκε’ ὤμοισι κλίναντες.
sentences.tr:
autar Achaioi
teicheos asson isan sake’ ōmoisi klinantes.
sentences.l:
but the Achaeans
closer to the wall were going, their shields on their shoulders leaning.
sentences.i: but the Achaeans drew nearer to the wall, their shields leaning on their shoulders.
sentences.n: Now the other side. αὐτὰρ Ἀχαιοί answers the μέν of the previous unit: the Trojans rest, but the Achaeans come on. ἆσσον is the comparative adverb ‘closer’ and takes the genitive τείχεος ‘to the wall’. ἴσαν is the imperfect of εἶμι ‘go’, third plural, so ‘were going’. σάκε’ is σάκεα ‘shields’ with its final vowel elided, and ὤμοισι the dative plural of ὦμος ‘shoulder’. κλίναντες is the aorist participle of κλίνω, ‘having leaned’ the shields on their shoulders, how the shields were carried is not said beyond that.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτορα δ’ αὐτοῦ μεῖναι ὀλοιὴ μοῖρα πέδησεν
Ἰλίου προπάροιθε πυλάων τε Σκαιάων.
sentences.tr:
Hektora d’ autou meinai oloiē moira pedēsen
Iliou proparoithe pylaōn te Skaiaōn.
sentences.l:
But Hector in that place to remain a baneful fate bound,
before Ilium and the Scaean Gates.
sentences.i: But a baneful fate had bound Hector to stay right there, in front of Ilium and the Scaean Gates.
sentences.n: Hector is the only Trojan left outside. ὀλοιή is the feminine of ὀλοιός, a variant of ὀλοός ‘baneful’, and μοῖρα ‘fate’ is the subject of πέδησεν, the aorist of πεδάω ‘bind, shackle’, from πέδη ‘fetter’. Ἕκτορα is its object, with the infinitive μεῖναι ‘to stay’ saying what the fate bound him to do. αὐτοῦ is an adverb, ‘right there’, and Ἰλίου προπάροιθε πυλάων τε Σκαιάων ‘in front of Ilium and of the Scaean Gates’ puts him at the Scaean Gates in the city wall; both nouns are genitives after the preposition-like προπάροιθε.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ Πηλείωνα προσηύδα Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων·
sentences.tr: autar Pēleiōna prosēuda Phoibos Apollōn·
sentences.l: But to the son of Peleus spoke Phoebus Apollo:
sentences.i: Then Phoebus Apollo spoke to the son of Peleus:
sentences.n: Apollo has been leading Achilles away from the city in a disguise (the end of Book 21 shows him luring Achilles with a trick), and now he speaks in his own person. Πηλείωνα is a patronymic in the accusative, ‘the son of Peleus’, here Achilles. προσηύδα is the imperfect of προσαυδάω ‘speak to’, with the dative-sense object in the accusative, and Φοῖβος Ἀπόλλων is the god’s two-part name. The unit ends at the colon that opens his speech, which runs to line 13.

sentences.t:
τίπτέ με Πηλέος υἱὲ ποσὶν ταχέεσσι διώκεις
αὐτὸς θνητὸς ἐὼν θεὸν ἄμβροτον;
sentences.tr:
tipte me Pēleos huie posin tacheessi diōkeis
autos thnētos eōn theon ambroton;
sentences.l:
“Why do you pursue me, son of Peleus, with swift feet,
yourself being mortal, a deathless god?
sentences.i: “Why do you chase me, son of Peleus, on your swift feet, you who are mortal, when I am a deathless god?
sentences.n: Apollo’s speech opens with a reproach. τίπτε is τί ποτε ‘why ever’ and με is ‘me’, the object of διώκεις ‘you pursue’. ποσὶν ταχέεσσι is ‘with swift feet’, the dative plural of ταχύς with the uncontracted ending -εσσι. θνητὸς ἐών ‘being mortal’ and θεὸν ἄμβροτον ‘a deathless god’ are set side by side; ἄμβροτος ‘deathless’ is the Greek word for the gods’ state. The object of διώκεις is με; θεὸν ἄμβροτον is in the accusative in apposition to it, and αὐτός ‘yourself’ stresses Achilles.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ νύ πώ με
ἔγνως ὡς θεός εἰμι, σὺ δ’ ἀσπερχὲς μενεαίνεις.
sentences.tr:
oude ny pō me
egnōs hōs theos eimi, sy d’ asperches meneaineis.
sentences.l:
And not yet me
have you known, that I am a god, and you are eager unceasingly.
sentences.i: You have not yet recognised that I am a god, and you are eager, without pause.
sentences.n: οὐδέ νύ πώ με ἔγνως ‘and you have not yet recognised me’; ἔγνως is the aorist of γιγνώσκω, and ὡς here means ‘that’. The verb μενεαίνεις ‘you are eager’ has no object: the Greek does not say eager for what, and it is understood from the chase. ἀσπερχές ‘unceasingly’ (‘without pause’ in the English) is the adverb that goes with μενεαίνω elsewhere in the poem.

sentences.t:
ἦ νύ τοι οὔ τι μέλει Τρώων πόνος, οὓς ἐφόβησας,
οἳ δή τοι εἰς ἄστυ ἄλεν, σὺ δὲ δεῦρο λιάσθης.
sentences.tr:
ē ny toi ou ti melei Trōōn ponos, hous ephobēsas,
hoi dē toi eis asty alen, sy de deuro liasthēs.
sentences.l:
Surely now to you it is no care, the toil of the Trojans, whom you put to flight,
who, you see, have been crowded into the town, while you here swerved aside.
sentences.i: Surely it is no concern of yours, the toil of the Trojans, whom you put to flight; they, you see, have been crowded into the town, while you have swerved aside to here.
sentences.n: ἦ νύ τοι οὔ τι μέλει ‘surely now it is no concern to you’: μέλει ‘is a care’ takes the dative τοι. Τρώων πόνος is ‘the toil of the Trojans’, and the Greek does not say whether it means the labour of fighting them or their own suffering. ἐφόβησας is the aorist of φοβέω ‘put to flight’. τοι in line 12 is the ‘you see’ particle (an ethic dative, not the relative), and ἄλεν is a third-plural aorist passive, ‘were crowded together’, from the same verb as ἀλέντες in Book 21. λιάσθης is the aorist passive of λιάζομαι ‘bend, swerve aside’, with δεῦρο ‘to here’.

sentences.t: οὐ μέν με κτενέεις, ἐπεὶ οὔ τοι μόρσιμός εἰμι.
sentences.tr: ou men me kteneeis, epei ou toi morsimos eimi.
sentences.l: Truly you will not kill me, since to you I am not destined.”
sentences.i: You will not kill me, for I am not one destined for you.”
sentences.n: The last line of Apollo’s speech. κτενέεις is the uncontracted future of κτείνω ‘kill’ (Attic κτενεῖς), and ἐπεί gives the reason. μόρσιμος means ‘destined, assigned by fate’; οὔ τοι μόρσιμός εἰμι means ‘I am not one fated for you’, that is, not a man whose death Achilles is destined to bring about. Apollo says the pursuit is pointless because a god cannot be killed; the speech ends with this line.

sentences.t: τὸν δὲ μέγ’ ὀχθήσας προσέφη πόδας ὠκὺς Ἀχιλλεύς·
sentences.tr: ton de meg’ ochthēsas prosephē podas ōkys Achilleus·
sentences.l: Him, greatly vexed, addressed swift-in-feet Achilles:
sentences.i: Greatly troubled, Achilles, swift of foot, said to him:
sentences.n: Achilles answers the god. The line is the stock reply formula for a hero who has been stung by what he heard: ὀχθήσας is the aorist participle of ὀχθέω ‘be troubled, vexed’, with μέγ’ ‘greatly’. τὸν δέ ‘and him’ is the article used as a pronoun, and προσέφη is the aorist of πρός + φημί, ‘addressed’. πόδας ὠκύς ‘swift in feet’ is the stock epithet, an accusative of respect. The speech runs to line 20.

sentences.t:
ἔβλαψάς μ’ ἑκάεργε θεῶν ὀλοώτατε πάντων
ἐνθάδε νῦν τρέψας ἀπὸ τείχεος· ἦ κ’ ἔτι πολλοὶ
γαῖαν ὀδὰξ εἷλον πρὶν Ἴλιον εἰσαφικέσθαι.
sentences.tr:
eblapsas m’ hekaerge theōn oloōtate pantōn
enthade nyn trepsas apo teicheos· ē k’ eti polloi
gaian odax heilon prin Ilion eisaphikesthai.
sentences.l:
“You have harmed me, far-working one, most baneful of all the gods,
here now having turned me away from the wall; surely still many
the earth with their teeth would have seized, before reaching Ilium.
sentences.i: “You have done me harm, you who work from afar, most baneful of all the gods, by turning me away from the wall to here. Surely many more would have bitten the earth before they reached Ilium.
sentences.n: Achilles knows at once which god it is. ἔβλαψας is the aorist of βλάπτω ‘harm, hinder’, and ἑκάεργε is the vocative of the god’s epithet, ‘far-working one’ (its meaning is disputed). ὀλοώτατε is the superlative of ὀλοός ‘baneful’, with the genitive θεῶν πάντων. ἐνθάδε … τρέψας ἀπὸ τείχεος ‘having turned me from the wall to here’ is the aorist participle of τρέπω. ἦ κ’ ἔτι πολλοί … εἷλον is ‘surely still many would have seized’: εἷλον is the aorist of αἱρέω, with κε giving the unreal ‘would have’, and γαῖαν ὀδάξ ‘the earth with their teeth’ is the picture of men dying with their mouths in the dust. εἰσαφικέσθαι is the aorist infinitive of εἰσαφικνέομαι ‘arrive at’.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ ἐμὲ μὲν μέγα κῦδος ἀφείλεο, τοὺς δὲ σάωσας
ῥηϊδίως, ἐπεὶ οὔ τι τίσιν γ’ ἔδεισας ὀπίσσω.
sentences.tr:
nyn d’ eme men mega kydos apheileo, tous de saōsas
rhēïdiōs, epei ou ti tisin g’ edeisas opissō.
sentences.l:
But now great glory you took from me, and them you saved
easily, since not at all vengeance did you fear hereafter.
sentences.i: But as it is, you have taken great glory from me and saved them easily, since you had no fear of any vengeance hereafter.
sentences.n: νῦν δέ ‘but as it is’ turns from what would have happened to what did. ἐμὲ μέν … τοὺς δέ sets ‘me’ against ‘them’, the Trojans; ἀφείλεο is the aorist middle of ἀφαιρέω ‘take away’ and σάωσας the aorist of σαόω ‘save’. ῥηϊδίως ‘easily’ is the epic form with ῥηϊ-. τίσις is ‘vengeance, requital’, and ὀπίσσω ‘afterwards’ looks to the future; γε stresses τίσιν, ‘vengeance at least’. Achilles complains that Apollo could act because no mortal can punish a god.

sentences.t: ἦ σ’ ἂν τισαίμην, εἴ μοι δύναμίς γε παρείη.
sentences.tr: ē s’ an tisaimēn, ei moi dynamis ge pareiē.
sentences.l: Truly I would take vengeance on you, if the power were at hand for me.”
sentences.i: I would take vengeance on you, if only I had the power.”
sentences.n: ἦ is ‘truly’. τισαίμην is the aorist optative middle of τίνυμαι ‘take vengeance on’ with ἄν, ‘I would take vengeance’, and εἴ … παρείη ‘if it were present’ (the optative of πάρειμι) with δύναμις ‘power’ is the condition. Together they make a remote condition (‘would … if … were’): he lacks the power, and the speech ends on that.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὼν προτὶ ἄστυ μέγα φρονέων ἐβεβήκει,
σευάμενος ὥς θ’ ἵππος ἀεθλοφόρος σὺν ὄχεσφιν,
sentences.tr:
hōs eipōn proti asty mega phroneōn ebebēkei,
seuamenos hōs th’ hippos aethlophoros syn ochesphin,
sentences.l:
So speaking, toward the town, greatly thinking, he had gone,
rushing like a prize-winning horse with its chariot,
sentences.i: So he spoke, and went toward the town full of proud thoughts, rushing like a prize-winning horse with its chariot,
sentences.n: The first of two units for one simile: Achilles runs for the city as a racehorse runs. ὣς εἰπών ‘having so spoken’; μέγα φρονέων is the stock ‘greatly thinking’, here ‘full of proud thoughts’. ἐβεβήκει is the pluperfect of βαίνω, used as a plain past, ‘went’. σευάμενος is the aorist middle participle of σεύω ‘rush’. ἀεθλοφόρος is literally ‘prize-bearing’ (ἆθλον ‘prize’ + φέρω), here ‘prize-winning’, a horse that wins the prize at the games, and ὄχεσφιν is the plural ὄχεα ‘chariot’ with the old ending -φιν, governed by σύν ‘with’.

sentences.t:
ὅς ῥά τε ῥεῖα θέῃσι τιταινόμενος πεδίοιο·
ὣς Ἀχιλεὺς λαιψηρὰ πόδας καὶ γούνατ’ ἐνώμα.
sentences.tr:
hos rha te rheia theēisi titainomenos pedioio·
hōs Achileus laipsēra podas kai gounat’ enōma.
sentences.l:
which easily runs, stretching itself, over the plain;
so Achilles quick his feet and knees plied.
sentences.i: which runs easily, at full stretch, across the plain; so Achilles plied his feet and knees quickly.
sentences.n: The simile’s relative clause, ὅς ῥά τε ῥεῖα θέῃσι: θέῃσι is the present subjunctive of θέω ‘run’, with the general sense ‘as it runs’, and ῥεῖα is ‘easily’. τιταινόμενος is the participle of τιταίνω ‘stretch’, ‘stretching itself’, and πεδίοιο is a genitive of the ground covered, ‘over the plain’. After the semicolon the poet returns to Achilles: ὣς Ἀχιλεύς ‘so Achilles’. λαιψηρά is an adverb, ‘quickly’, and ἐνώμα the imperfect of νωμάω ‘ply’, so he worked his feet and knees as the horse its legs.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ὃ γέρων Πρίαμος πρῶτος ἴδεν ὀφθαλμοῖσι
παμφαίνονθ’ ὥς τ’ ἀστέρ’ ἐπεσσύμενον πεδίοιο,
sentences.tr:
ton d’ ho gerōn Priamos prōtos iden ophthalmoisi
pamphainonth’ hōs t’ aster’ epessymenon pedioio,
sentences.l:
Him the old man Priam first saw with his eyes,
all-shining like a star, rushing over the plain,
sentences.i: Old Priam was the first to see him with his eyes, shining all over like a star as he rushed across the plain,
sentences.n: From the wall, Priam looks down and sees Achilles coming. τὸν δ’ ὃ γέρων Πρίαμος: the article τόν is ‘him’, and ὃ γέρων is ‘he, the old man’ (the edition prints ὃ with an accent, as a pronoun). παμφαίνονθ’ is παμφαίνοντα, the accusative participle ‘shining all over’, agreeing with τόν; ἐπεσσύμενον is the participle of ἐπισεύομαι ‘rush at’. The star simile begins here and fills the next unit: it is the star of line 29.

sentences.t:
ὅς ῥά τ’ ὀπώρης εἶσιν, ἀρίζηλοι δέ οἱ αὐγαὶ
φαίνονται πολλοῖσι μετ’ ἀστράσι νυκτὸς ἀμολγῷ,
ὅν τε κύν’ Ὠρίωνος ἐπίκλησιν καλέουσι.
sentences.tr:
hos rha t’ opōrēs eisin, arizēloi de hoi augai
phainontai polloisi met’ astrasi nyktos amolgōi,
hon te kyn’ Ōriōnos epiklēsin kaleousi.
sentences.l:
which goes forth in late summer, and conspicuous its glare
appears among many stars in the dead of night,
which they by name call the dog of Orion.
sentences.i: which comes forth in late summer, and its glare is conspicuous among the many stars in the depths of the night; the star they call by name the dog of Orion.
sentences.n: The poem calls the star the dog of Orion and does not name it further; it is traditionally identified with Sirius. ὀπώρης is a genitive of time, ‘in the late summer’ (ὀπώρα is the fruit season at summer’s end). αὐγαί is plural and collective, ‘glare’; ἀρίζηλοι ‘conspicuous’. ἀμολγός is of unknown meaning: νυκτὸς ἀμολγῷ is a fixed phrase of ‘night’, and ‘milking-time’ and ‘darkness’ are the ancient guesses; the English keeps ‘depths of the night’, as elsewhere in the poem. ἐπίκλησιν is an accusative adverb, ‘by name, as a surname’, and καλέουσι the uncontracted ‘they call’.

sentences.t:
λαμπρότατος μὲν ὅ γ’ ἐστί, κακὸν δέ τε σῆμα τέτυκται,
καί τε φέρει πολλὸν πυρετὸν δειλοῖσι βροτοῖσιν·
sentences.tr:
lamprotatos men ho g’ esti, kakon de te sēma tetyktai,
kai te pherei pollon pyreton deiloisi brotoisin·
sentences.l:
Brightest indeed it is, but an evil sign it has been made,
and it brings much fever to miserable mortals;
sentences.i: It is the brightest of stars, but it has been made an evil sign, and it brings much fever to miserable mortals;
sentences.n: The simile’s point: the star is bright, and an omen of harm. λαμπρότατος is the superlative, ‘brightest’; ὅ γε ‘it’ is the star. τέτυκται is the perfect passive of τεύχω, ‘has been made’, and σῆμα is ‘sign’. The τε in κακὸν δέ τε σῆμα and καί τε φέρει marks a general statement. πυρετός is ‘burning heat, fever’, an accusative with πολλόν (πολύ) ‘much’. δειλοῖσι βροτοῖσιν ‘miserable mortals’ is a fixed pair, and the phrase returns at line 76.

sentences.t: ὣς τοῦ χαλκὸς ἔλαμπε περὶ στήθεσσι θέοντος.
sentences.tr: hōs tou chalkos elampe peri stēthessi theontos.
sentences.l: so of him the bronze shone about his chest as he ran.
sentences.i: so the bronze shone about his chest as he ran.
sentences.n: The simile is closed: Achilles’ armour gleams like the star, and like the star it is a bad sign for the Trojans. ὣς … ἔλαμπε ‘so it shone’; τοῦ is the genitive ‘his’, and χαλκός is the bronze of the armour. θέοντος is the genitive participle of θέω ‘run’, in agreement with τοῦ. The same line occurs earlier in the poem, and its English is the same there.

sentences.t:
ᾤμωξεν δ’ ὃ γέρων, κεφαλὴν δ’ ὅ γε κόψατο χερσὶν
ὑψόσ’ ἀνασχόμενος, μέγα δ’ οἰμώξας ἐγεγώνει,
sentences.tr:
ōimōxen d’ ho gerōn, kephalēn d’ ho ge kopsato chersin
hypsos’ anaschomenos, mega d’ oimōxas egegōnei,
sentences.l:
And the old man wailed aloud, and his head he struck with his hands,
raising them high, and, greatly wailing, called out
sentences.i: The old man cried out aloud and struck his head with his hands, holding them high, and, wailing greatly, he called out
sentences.n: Priam’s reaction. ᾤμωξεν is the aorist of οἰμώζω ‘cry out in grief’, and κόψατο the aorist middle of κόπτω, ‘struck (his own head)’. ὑψόσ’ is ὑψόσε ‘upward’, and ἀνασχόμενος the aorist middle participle of ἀνέχω, ‘holding up’ (his hands). οἰμώξας ‘having cried out’ with μέγα ‘greatly’ gives the loud lament. ἐγεγώνει is a pluperfect of γεγωνέω ‘call out’ with the sense of an imperfect, ‘kept calling out’.

sentences.t:
λισσόμενος φίλον υἱόν· ὃ δὲ προπάροιθε πυλάων
ἑστήκει ἄμοτον μεμαὼς Ἀχιλῆϊ μάχεσθαι·
sentences.tr:
lissomenos philon huion· ho de proparoithe pylaōn
hestēkei amoton memaōs Achilēï machesthai·
sentences.l:
begging his dear son; but he in front of the gates
stood, unceasingly eager to fight Achilles;
sentences.i: begging his dear son; but Hector stood in front of the gates, eager without ceasing to fight Achilles;
sentences.n: λισσόμενος ‘begging’ takes the accusative φίλον υἱόν; the son is Hector. ὃ δέ ‘but he’ turns to Hector, who stands ἑστήκει (pluperfect of ἵστημι, ‘was standing’) in front of the gates. μεμαώς is the perfect participle of μαίομαι, ‘eager’, with the infinitive μάχεσθαι ‘to fight’ and the dative Ἀχιλῆϊ. ἄμοτον is an adverb whose meaning is not known; ‘without ceasing’ is the traditional guess.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ὃ γέρων ἐλεεινὰ προσηύδα χεῖρας ὀρεγνύς·
sentences.tr: ton d’ ho gerōn eleeina prosēuda cheiras oregnys·
sentences.l: and him the old man pitiably addressed, stretching out his hands:
sentences.i: and the old man, stretching out his hands, spoke pitiably to him:
sentences.n: This line introduces Priam’s speech (38–76). ἐλεεινά is an adverb, ‘pitiably’, and προσηύδα ‘addressed’; τὸν δ’ ὁ γέρων again has the article as a pronoun, ‘him’. ὀρεγνύς is the present participle of ὀρέγνυμι ‘stretch out’, and the gesture belongs to a plea from the wall.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτορ μή μοι μίμνε φίλον τέκος ἀνέρα τοῦτον
οἶος ἄνευθ’ ἄλλων, ἵνα μὴ τάχα πότμον ἐπίσπῃς,
sentences.tr:
Hektor mē moi mimne philon tekos anera touton
oios aneuth’ allōn, hina mē tacha potmon epispēis,
sentences.l:
“Hector, do not, for me, wait for this man, dear child,
alone, away from the others, so that you may not soon meet your doom
sentences.i: “Hector, my dear child, do not, for my sake, wait for this man alone, away from the others, or you may soon meet your doom,
sentences.n: Priam’s speech runs to line 76: first a plea, then a picture of what awaits him if Hector dies. μή … μίμνε ‘do not wait for’ is a negative imperative, and μοι ‘for me’ is an ethic dative: ‘for my sake’. ἀνέρα τοῦτον ‘this man’ is Achilles, named only by pointing. οἶος ‘alone’ and ἄνευθ’ ἄλλων ‘apart from others’ say that no Trojan will stand beside him. ἵνα μή with the subjunctive ἐπίσπῃς is ‘so that you may not meet’, the aorist of ἐφέπω, and πότμον ‘doom’; τάχα ‘soon’.

sentences.t:
Πηλεΐωνι δαμείς, ἐπεὶ ἦ πολὺ φέρτερός ἐστι
σχέτλιος·
sentences.tr:
Pēleïōni dameis, epei ē poly pherteros esti
schetlios·
sentences.l:
overcome by the son of Peleus, since he is truly much stronger,
the cruel one;
sentences.i: and be overcome by the son of Peleus, since he is far the stronger, the cruel one;
sentences.n: δαμείς is the aorist passive participle of δάμνημι ‘overcome’, ‘overcome’, with the agent Πηλεΐωνι in the dative. ἦ πολὺ φέρτερος is ‘truly much stronger’: φέρτερος is the comparative of ἀγαθός ‘better, stronger’. σχέτλιος is ‘cruel one’, a word of reproach whose force here is ‘hard, pitiless’, said of Achilles.

sentences.t:
αἴθε θεοῖσι φίλος τοσσόνδε γένοιτο
ὅσσον ἐμοί·
sentences.tr:
aithe theoisi philos tossonde genoito
hosson emoi·
sentences.l:
Would that to the gods dear he might become
so much as to me;
sentences.i: If only he were as dear to the gods as he is to me;
sentences.n: αἴθε … γένοιτο is a wish, ‘would that he might become’. φίλος ‘dear’ is bitter: Priam hates Achilles, and the wish is that the gods would hate him as Priam does. The next line says what would follow: dogs and vultures eating him. τοσσόνδε … ὅσσον is the pair ‘so much … as’, and ἐμοί is ‘to me’.

sentences.t:
τάχα κέν ἑ κύνες καὶ γῦπες ἔδοιεν
κείμενον· ἦ κέ μοι αἰνὸν ἀπὸ πραπίδων ἄχος ἔλθοι·
sentences.tr:
tacha ken he kynes kai gypes edoien
keimenon· ē ke moi ainon apo prapidōn achos elthoi·
sentences.l:
soon the dogs and vultures would eat him
lying dead; truly from my midriff a terrible grief would go.
sentences.i: The dogs and vultures would soon eat him as he lay there, and a terrible grief would leave my heart.
sentences.n: τάχα κέν … ἔδοιεν is a potential, ‘would soon eat’; ἔδοιεν is the optative of ἔδω ‘eat’, and ἑ is the old pronoun ‘him’. κείμενον ‘lying (dead)’ agrees with it. ἦ κέ … ἔλθοι ‘truly would go’: ἄχος ‘grief’ is the subject and ἀπὸ πραπίδων ‘from the midriff’ the place, the diaphragm region that Homer treats as the seat of feeling. αἰνόν ‘terrible’ is a stock word of dread.

sentences.t:
ὅς μ’ υἱῶν πολλῶν τε καὶ ἐσθλῶν εὖνιν ἔθηκε
κτείνων καὶ περνὰς νήσων ἔπι τηλεδαπάων.
sentences.tr:
hos m’ huiōn pollōn te kai esthlōn eunin ethēke
kteinōn kai pernas nēsōn epi tēledapaōn.
sentences.l:
who has made me bereft of sons, many and noble,
killing and selling them to far-off islands.
sentences.i: He has left me without my sons, many and noble, killing them and selling them to far-off islands.
sentences.n: ὅς ‘who’ is Achilles, and ἔθηκε is the aorist of τίθημι, ‘made’. εὖνις ‘bereft of’ takes the genitive υἱῶν. κτείνων and περνάς are present participles: κτείνων ‘killing’ and περνάς (from πέρνημι, a verb for selling, here the nominative masculine) ‘selling’, the two verbs name the two things Achilles did to his sons. νήσων ἔπι τηλεδαπάων is ‘to far-off islands’; ἔπι follows the noun it governs.

sentences.t:
καὶ γὰρ νῦν δύο παῖδε Λυκάονα καὶ Πολύδωρον
οὐ δύναμαι ἰδέειν Τρώων εἰς ἄστυ ἀλέντων,
τούς μοι Λαοθόη τέκετο κρείουσα γυναικῶν.
sentences.tr:
kai gar nyn dyo paide Lykaona kai Polydōron
ou dynamai ideein Trōōn eis asty alentōn,
tous moi Laothoē teketo kreiousa gynaikōn.
sentences.l:
For even now two sons, Lycaon and Polydorus,
I cannot see among the Trojans crowded into the town,
whom to me Laothoe bore, ruling among women.
sentences.i: For even now I cannot see my two sons, Lycaon and Polydorus, among the Trojans who have crowded into the town, the sons Laothoe bore me, a queen among women.
sentences.n: Priam does not yet know that both sons are dead: the reader has seen Polydorus die in Book 20 and Lycaon in Book 21. καὶ γὰρ νῦν ‘for even now’; δύο παῖδε is a dual, ‘two sons’, and δύναμαι ἰδέειν ‘I am able to see’ (ἰδέειν is the epic infinitive). Τρώων … ἀλέντων is a genitive absolute-like phrase, ‘the Trojans having been crowded together’ (as at 12). τούς is the relative ‘whom’, τέκετο the aorist middle of τίκτω ‘bore’, and Laothoe is a daughter of Altes, as Lycaon himself said in Book 21 (21.84–85). κρείουσα is the feminine of κρείων ‘ruling’, and γυναικῶν ‘among women’ is a genitive.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ εἰ μὲν ζώουσι μετὰ στρατῷ, ἦ τ’ ἂν ἔπειτα
χαλκοῦ τε χρυσοῦ τ’ ἀπολυσόμεθ’, ἔστι γὰρ ἔνδον·
sentences.tr:
all’ ei men zōousi meta stratōi, ē t’ an epeita
chalkou te chrysou t’ apolysometh’, esti gar endon·
sentences.l:
But if they are alive among the army, then surely
with bronze and gold we shall ransom them, for there is some within;
sentences.i: But if they are alive in the army, then we shall ransom them with bronze and gold, for there is some inside;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ εἰ μέν … ‘but if indeed’ opens the first of two possibilities (the second is at 52). ζώουσι is the uncontracted ‘they are alive’, and μετὰ στρατῷ ‘in the army’ evidently means the Achaean army, since the sons are not among the Trojans in the city (47): Priam is thinking of captives. ἦ τ’ ἄν ἔπειτα is ‘then surely’. ἀπολυσόμεθα is the future middle of ἀπολύω, ‘we shall ransom’, with χαλκοῦ τε χρυσοῦ τε as a genitive of price. ἔστι … ἔνδον ‘there is some within’ leaves the object unsaid; line 51 explains it.

sentences.t: πολλὰ γὰρ ὤπασε παιδὶ γέρων ὀνομάκλυτος Ἄλτης.
sentences.tr: polla gar ōpase paidi gerōn onomaklytos Altēs.
sentences.l: for many things gave to his child the old man of famous name, Altes.
sentences.i: for old Altes, a man of famous name, gave his daughter many things.
sentences.n: Altes is the father of Laothoe; Lycaon named him as his mother Laothoe’s father in Book 21 (21.84–85). ὤπασε is the aorist of ὀπάζω ‘give, bestow’, with πολλά ‘many things’ as object and παιδί ‘to his child’, here a daughter. γέρων ὀνομάκλυτος is ‘old man of famous name’; ὀνομάκλυτος is ὄνομα ‘name’ + κλυτός ‘heard of, famous’.

sentences.t:
εἰ δ’ ἤδη τεθνᾶσι καὶ εἰν Ἀΐδαο δόμοισιν,
ἄλγος ἐμῷ θυμῷ καὶ μητέρι τοὶ τεκόμεσθα·
sentences.tr:
ei d’ ēdē tethnasi kai ein Aïdao domoisin,
algos emōi thymōi kai mēteri toi tekomestha·
sentences.l:
But if already they are dead and in the houses of Hades,
grief to my heart and to their mother, we who begot them;
sentences.i: But if they are already dead and in the house of Hades, there will be grief for my heart and for their mother, we who begot them;
sentences.n: εἰ δ’ ἤδη τεθνᾶσι is the second possibility: τεθνᾶσι is the perfect of θνῄσκω, ‘they are dead’. εἰν is a form of ἐν ‘in’ (as in εἰνί), and Ἀΐδαο δόμοισιν ‘in the houses of Hades’ is the world of the dead. ἄλγος is a noun with no verb of its own; ἔσσεται (‘will be’) at the start of line 55 serves both clauses. τοὶ τεκόμεσθα is ‘we who begot’, the aorist middle of τίκτω, with τοί as the relative pronoun οἵ. The mother is Laothoe.

sentences.t:
λαοῖσιν δ’ ἄλλοισι μινυνθαδιώτερον ἄλγος
ἔσσεται, ἢν μὴ καὶ σὺ θάνῃς Ἀχιλῆϊ δαμασθείς.
sentences.tr:
laoisin d’ alloisi minynthadiōteron algos
essetai, ēn mē kai sy thanēis Achilēï damastheis.
sentences.l:
but to the other people shorter-lived grief
will be, if you do not die too, overcome by Achilles.
sentences.i: but for the rest of the people the grief will be shorter-lived, unless you die as well, overcome by Achilles.
sentences.n: λαοῖσιν δ’ ἄλλοισι ‘but for the other people’. μινυνθαδιώτερον is the comparative of μινυνθάδιος ‘short-lived’, ‘shorter-lived’. ἔσσεται is the epic future of εἰμί ‘will be’. ἢν μὴ καὶ σὺ θάνῃς is ‘if you do not also die’: ἤν = ἐάν + the aorist subjunctive of θνῄσκω. Ἀχιλῆϊ δαμασθείς ‘overcome by Achilles’ is an aorist passive participle, as at 40.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ εἰσέρχεο τεῖχος ἐμὸν τέκος, ὄφρα σαώσῃς
Τρῶας καὶ Τρῳάς, μὴ δὲ μέγα κῦδος ὀρέξῃς
Πηλεΐδῃ, αὐτὸς δὲ φίλης αἰῶνος ἀμερθῇς.
sentences.tr:
all’ eisercheo teichos emon tekos, ophra saōsēis
Trōas kai Trōias, mē de mega kydos orexēis
Pēleïdēi, autos de philēs aiōnos amerthēis.
sentences.l:
But enter the wall, my child, so that you may save
the Trojan men and the Trojan women, and not great glory offer
to Peleus’-son, and yourself of your dear life be deprived.
sentences.i: But come inside the wall, my child, so that you may save the Trojan men and women, and not offer great glory to the son of Peleus, and be robbed of your own dear life.
sentences.n: The plea becomes a command. εἰσέρχεο is the imperative of εἰσέρχομαι ‘go in’, and ὄφρα σαώσῃς is a purpose clause, ‘so that you may save’. Τρῶας καὶ Τρῳάς ‘Trojan men and Trojan women’ (the second is an accusative plural). μὴ δέ ‘and not’ continues the purpose: ὀρέξῃς is the aorist subjunctive of ὀρέγω ‘stretch out, offer’, with Πηλεΐδῃ ‘to the son of Peleus’. ἀμερθῇς is the aorist passive subjunctive of ἀμέρδω, ‘be deprived of’, with the genitive φίλης αἰῶνος ‘dear life’.

sentences.t:
πρὸς δ’ ἐμὲ τὸν δύστηνον ἔτι φρονέοντ’ ἐλέησον
δύσμορον, ὅν ῥα πατὴρ Κρονίδης ἐπὶ γήραος οὐδῷ
αἴσῃ ἐν ἀργαλέῃ φθίσει κακὰ πόλλ’ ἐπιδόντα,
sentences.tr:
pros d’ eme ton dystēnon eti phroneont’ eleēson
dysmoron, hon rha patēr Kronidēs epi gēraos oudōi
aisēi en argaleēi phthisei kaka poll’ epidonta,
sentences.l:
And besides, me, the wretched one, still thinking, pity,
the ill-fated, whom the father, the son-of-Cronus, on the threshold of old age
in grievous fate will destroy, after I have seen many evils,
sentences.i: And pity me besides, wretched as I am, while I still have my wits, an ill-fated man, whom the father, the son of Cronus, will destroy on the threshold of old age by a grievous fate, when I have seen many evils,
sentences.n: πρὸς δ’ ἐμέ ‘and besides, me’; τὸν δύστηνον ‘the wretched one’ with the article for emphasis, and ἔτι φρονέοντα ‘still thinking’, that is, while still in his senses. ἐλέησον is the aorist imperative of ἐλεέω ‘pity’. πατὴρ Κρονίδης ‘the father, son of Cronus’ is Zeus. γήραος οὐδῷ is ‘the threshold of old age’, the edge of it. φθίσει is the future of φθίω ‘destroy’, and αἴσῃ ἐν ἀργαλέῃ ‘in a grievous fate’. ἐπιδόντα is the aorist participle of ἐφοράω, ‘having looked on’, agreeing with ὅν, the same man.

sentences.t:
υἷάς τ’ ὀλλυμένους ἑλκηθείσας τε θύγατρας,
καὶ θαλάμους κεραϊζομένους, καὶ νήπια τέκνα,
sentences.tr:
huias t’ ollymenous helkētheisas te thygatras,
kai thalamous keraïzomenous, kai nēpia tekna,
sentences.l:
my sons being destroyed and my daughters dragged off,
and the chambers being ravaged, and infant children
sentences.i: my sons being killed and my daughters dragged off, and the chambers ravaged, and the little children
sentences.n: These lines list what Priam will have seen; the participles depend on ἐπιδόντα in line 61. υἷάς is υἱούς ‘sons’, and ὀλλυμένους the present middle participle of ὄλλυμι ‘be destroyed’. ἑλκηθείσας is the aorist passive participle of ἕλκω ‘drag’, feminine because it agrees with θύγατρας ‘daughters’. θαλάμους κεραϊζομένους ‘chambers being ravaged’ (κεραΐζω ‘lay waste, plunder’), then νήπια τέκνα ‘infant children’, whose participle comes in the next line.

sentences.t:
βαλλόμενα προτὶ γαίῃ ἐν αἰνῇ δηϊοτῆτι,
ἑλκομένας τε νυοὺς ὀλοῇς ὑπὸ χερσὶν Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.tr:
ballomena proti gaiēi en ainēi dēïotēti,
helkomenas te nyous oloēis hypo chersin Achaiōn.
sentences.l:
flung to the ground in terrible slaughter,
and daughters-in-law dragged off under the baneful hands of the Achaeans.
sentences.i: flung to the ground in the terrible slaughter, and my sons’ wives dragged off under the baneful hands of the Achaeans.
sentences.n: βαλλόμενα is the present passive participle of βάλλω ‘throw’, neuter plural to agree with τέκνα; προτὶ γαίῃ is ‘to the ground’. δηϊοτής is ‘hostile fighting, slaughter’, and αἰνῇ ‘terrible’. νυούς, the accusative plural of νυός ‘daughter-in-law’ (a son’s wife), is the object of the participle ἑλκομένας ‘being dragged’. ὀλοῇς ὑπὸ χερσίν ‘under baneful hands’ keeps the stock ‘baneful’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὸν δ’ ἂν πύματόν με κύνες πρώτῃσι θύρῃσιν
ὠμησταὶ ἐρύουσιν, ἐπεί κέ τις ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ
τύψας ἠὲ βαλὼν ῥεθέων ἐκ θυμὸν ἕληται,
sentences.tr:
auton d’ an pymaton me kynes prōtēisi thyrēisin
ōmēstai eryousin, epei ke tis oxeï chalkōi
typsas ēe balōn rhetheōn ek thymon helētai,
sentences.l:
and me myself, last of all, the dogs at the front doors,
raw-feeding, will drag, after someone with sharp bronze
having struck or having thrown has taken the life from my limbs,
sentences.i: and me myself, last of all, the dogs that feed on raw flesh will drag at my front doors, after some man has struck or thrown at me with sharp bronze and taken the life from my limbs,
sentences.n: αὐτὸν δ’ ἂν πύματόν με ‘and me myself, last’: Priam is the last of his family to fall. The verb is ἐρύουσιν ‘they will drag’, and ἄν goes with it: the form may be read as a future or as a subjunctive with a short vowel, and either way the sense is ‘will drag’, once the ἐπεί-clause has happened. κύνες ‘dogs’ is the subject and ὠμησταί ‘raw-feeding’ describes it; πρώτῃσι θύρῃσιν is ‘at the first (outer) doors’. ἐπεί κε … ἕληται is ‘after … has taken’, the aorist subjunctive middle of αἱρέω. ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ ‘with sharp bronze’; τύψας and βαλών are aorist participles, ‘having struck’ and ‘having thrown’ (a spear); ῥεθέων is ‘limbs’ and θυμόν here ‘life’.

sentences.t:
οὓς τρέφον ἐν μεγάροισι τραπεζῆας θυραωρούς,
οἵ κ’ ἐμὸν αἷμα πιόντες ἀλύσσοντες περὶ θυμῷ
κείσοντ’ ἐν προθύροισι.
sentences.tr:
hous trephon en megaroisi trapezēas thyraōrous,
hoi k’ emon haima piontes alyssontes peri thymōi
keisont’ en prothyroisi.
sentences.l:
which I fed in the halls, table-dogs, door-guards,
they, my blood having drunk, frenzied in heart,
will lie in the forecourt.
sentences.i: The dogs I fed in my halls, my table-dogs and door-guards, having drunk my blood, frenzied at heart, will lie in the forecourt.
sentences.n: οὓς τρέφον ‘which I fed’ points back to the dogs; τρέφον is the imperfect of τρέφω, ‘I used to feed’. τραπεζῆας is ‘table-dogs’ (dogs fed from the table), and θυραωρούς ‘door-guards’. οἵ κ’ … πιόντες ‘they, having drunk’: πιόντες is the aorist participle of πίνω, ‘having drunk’, with ἐμὸν αἷμα ‘my blood’. ἀλύσσοντες is ‘frenzied’, and περὶ θυμῷ ‘at heart’ is a phrase whose περί (‘greatly’?) is not certain. κείσοντ’ is κείσονται, the future of κεῖμαι ‘lie’, and ἐν προθύροισι ‘in the forecourt’. The unit ends at the full stop in mid-line.

sentences.t:
νέῳ δέ τε πάντ’ ἐπέοικεν
ἄρηϊ κταμένῳ δεδαϊγμένῳ ὀξέϊ χαλκῷ
κεῖσθαι·
sentences.tr:
neōi de te pant’ epeoiken
arēï ktamenōi dedaïgmenōi oxeï chalkōi
keisthai·
sentences.i: For a young man everything is seemly, killed in war and torn by sharp bronze, to lie there;
sentences.n: Priam turns to the contrast: a young man’s death is fair, an old man’s is not. νέῳ ‘for a young man’ takes πάντ’ ἐπέοικεν ‘everything is fitting’. ἄρηϊ is the dative of ἄρης, ‘war’ (the god’s name used for what he stands for), with κταμένῳ, the aorist participle of κτείνω, ‘killed’. δεδαϊγμένῳ is the perfect passive participle of δαΐζω ‘cut up, tear’. κεῖσθαι ‘to lie’ is the infinitive that everything fits: lying dead.

sentences.t: πάντα δὲ καλὰ θανόντι περ ὅττι φανήῃ·
sentences.tr: panta de kala thanonti per hotti phanēēi·
sentences.l: and fair is all, to one dead though he be, whatever shows;
sentences.i: and all that shows is fair, though he is dead;
sentences.n: πάντα δὲ καλά ‘and all things are fair’. θανόντι περ is the aorist participle of θνῄσκω with the intensifying περ, ‘though dead’, and ὅττι (= ὅ τι) φανήῃ ‘whatever appears’ is the aorist passive subjunctive of φαίνω, ‘may be seen’. The point is that a young warrior, even dead, is a fine sight, whatever is shown of him.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ πολιόν τε κάρη πολιόν τε γένειον
αἰδῶ τ’ αἰσχύνωσι κύνες κταμένοιο γέροντος,
τοῦτο δὴ οἴκτιστον πέλεται δειλοῖσι βροτοῖσιν.
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē polion te karē polion te geneion
aidō t’ aischynōsi kynes ktamenoio gerontos,
touto dē oiktiston peletai deiloisi brotoisin.
sentences.l:
But when the grey head and the grey beard
and the shame the dogs disfigure of a slain old man,
this indeed is the most lamentable thing that comes to miserable mortals.”
sentences.i: But when dogs disfigure the grey head and the grey beard and the shame of an old man who has been killed, that is the most lamentable thing that comes to miserable mortals.”
sentences.n: The picture Priam fears for himself. πολιὸν τε κάρη πολιόν τε γένειον ‘the grey head and the grey beard’, then αἰδῶ τ’, the accusative of αἰδώς ‘shame’, which is generally taken here to mean the private parts, the part that modesty covers. αἰσχύνωσι is the subjunctive of αἰσχύνω ‘disfigure, shame’ with ὅτε, and κύνες ‘dogs’ is its subject; κταμένοιο γέροντος is the genitive ‘of a slain old man’. οἴκτιστον is the superlative of οἰκτρός, ‘most lamentable’. This line closes Priam’s speech.

sentences.t:
ἦ ῥ’ ὃ γέρων, πολιὰς δ’ ἄρ’ ἀνὰ τρίχας ἕλκετο χερσὶ
τίλλων ἐκ κεφαλῆς· οὐδ’ Ἕκτορι θυμὸν ἔπειθε.
sentences.tr:
ē rh’ ho gerōn, polias d’ ar’ ana trichas helketo chersi
tillōn ek kephalēs· oud’ Hektori thymon epeithe.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, the old man, and the grey hairs he was pulling up with his hands,
tearing them from his head; but not Hector’s heart did he persuade.
sentences.i: So the old man spoke, and with his hands he pulled up his grey hair, tearing it from his head; but he did not persuade the heart of Hector.
sentences.n: ἦ ῥ’ is ἦ ῥα ‘so he spoke’, a formula at the end of a speech. ἕλκετο is the imperfect middle of ἕλκω ‘pull’, with ἀνά ‘up’ (a split compound), and τίλλων ‘plucking’ is the present participle. πολιὰς … τρίχας ‘grey hairs’. οὐδ’ Ἕκτορι θυμὸν ἔπειθε: ἔπειθε is an imperfect, ‘was not persuading’, a failed attempt, and Ἕκτορι is the dative of possession with θυμόν, ‘Hector’s heart’.

sentences.t:
μήτηρ δ’ αὖθ’ ἑτέρωθεν ὀδύρετο δάκρυ χέουσα
κόλπον ἀνιεμένη, ἑτέρηφι δὲ μαζὸν ἀνέσχε·
sentences.tr:
mētēr d’ auth’ heterōthen odyreto dakry cheousa
kolpon aniemenē, heterēphi de mazon anesche·
sentences.l:
And the mother in turn from the other side lamented, a tear shedding,
her bosom loosening, and with the other hand she held out her breast;
sentences.i: His mother in turn wept on the other side, shedding tears, loosening the fold of her robe, and with her other hand she held out her breast;
sentences.n: The mother is Hector’s mother, Hecuba, who is not named in these lines. ὀδύρετο is the imperfect middle of ὀδύρομαι ‘lament’, and ἑτέρωθεν ‘from the other side’ sets her over against Priam. δάκρυ χέουσα ‘shedding a tear’ is a stock phrase. κόλπον ἀνιεμένη ‘loosening the fold’ is the participle of ἀνίημι, the fold being the part of the robe over the breast. ἑτέρηφι is ‘with the other (hand)’, and μαζὸν ἀνέσχε ‘held out her breast’ the aorist of ἀνέχω; she bares the breast that nursed him.

sentences.t: καί μιν δάκρυ χέουσ’ ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr: kai min dakry cheous’ epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.l: and to him, a tear shedding, winged words she spoke:
sentences.i: and, shedding tears, she spoke winged words to him:
sentences.n: A reply-formula line that opens Hecuba’s speech (82–89). μιν is ‘him’, Hector. ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα ‘she spoke winged words’ is the stock phrase, ‘winged words’ being, on the usual explanation, words that fly from speaker to hearer. δάκρυ χέουσ’ is χέουσα with its final vowel elided, ‘shedding a tear’.

sentences.t:
Ἕκτορ τέκνον ἐμὸν τάδε τ’ αἴδεο καί μ’ ἐλέησον
αὐτήν, εἴ ποτέ τοι λαθικηδέα μαζὸν ἐπέσχον·
sentences.tr:
Hektor teknon emon tade t’ aideo kai m’ eleēson
autēn, ei pote toi lathikēdea mazon epeschon·
sentences.l:
“Hector, my child, respect these things and pity me
myself, if ever to you the care-forgetting breast I held out;
sentences.i: “Hector, my child, show respect for this, and take pity on me myself, if ever I held out to you the breast that made you forget your cares;
sentences.n: Hecuba’s plea is the bared breast. τάδε αἴδεο ‘respect these things’: αἴδεο is the imperative of αἰδέομαι ‘feel shame before, respect’, and the things are the gesture just made. καί μ’ ἐλέησον αὐτήν is ‘and pity me myself’. εἴ ποτέ … ἐπέσχον ‘if ever I held out’ is the aorist of ἐπέχω, with τοι ‘to you’. λαθικηδής means ‘making cares forgotten’ (λήθω + κῆδος), said of the nursing breast.

sentences.t:
τῶν μνῆσαι φίλε τέκνον ἄμυνε δὲ δήϊον ἄνδρα
τείχεος ἐντὸς ἐών, μὴ δὲ πρόμος ἵστασο τούτῳ
σχέτλιος·
sentences.tr:
tōn mnēsai phile teknon amyne de dēïon andra
teicheos entos eōn, mē de promos histaso toutōi
schetlios·
sentences.i: Remember these things, dear child, and ward off the enemy from inside the wall, and do not take your stand against him as a champion, cruel one;
sentences.n: τῶν μνῆσαι ‘remember those things’: μνῆσαι is the aorist imperative middle of μιμνήσκομαι, with the genitive. ἄμυνε is ‘ward off’, with δήϊον ἄνδρα ‘the hostile man’, and τείχεος ἐντὸς ἐών ‘being inside the wall’. μὴ δέ … ἵστασο is ‘and do not stand’, a middle imperative of ἵστημι, and πρόμος is a foremost fighter, ‘as a champion’; τούτῳ ‘against him’ is dative. σχέτλιος ‘cruel one’ is said to Hector as a reproach: hard on his parents.

sentences.t:
εἴ περ γάρ σε κατακτάνῃ, οὔ σ’ ἔτ’ ἔγωγε
κλαύσομαι ἐν λεχέεσσι φίλον θάλος, ὃν τέκον αὐτή,
sentences.tr:
ei per gar se kataktanēi, ou s’ et’ egōge
klausomai en lecheessi philon thalos, hon tekon autē,
sentences.l:
for if he kills you, no longer will I
mourn you on beds, dear shoot, whom I bore myself,
sentences.i: for if he kills you, I shall no longer weep for you laid on a bier, my dear scion, whom I bore myself,
sentences.n: εἴ περ γάρ ‘for if’ with κατακτάνῃ, the aorist subjunctive of κατακτείνω ‘kill’. κλαύσομαι is the future of κλαίω, ‘I shall weep for’, with the object σε in the same clause (σ’ ἔτ’). ἐν λεχέεσσι is ‘on beds’, plural, meaning the bier on which the dead are laid out for mourning. θάλος is ‘shoot, scion’, a child as a growing branch, and ὃν τέκον αὐτή ‘whom I bore myself’ is the aorist of τίκτω.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἄλοχος πολύδωρος· ἄνευθε δέ σε μέγα νῶϊν
Ἀργείων παρὰ νηυσὶ κύνες ταχέες κατέδονται.
sentences.tr:
oud’ alochos polydōros· aneuthe de se mega nōïn
Argeiōn para nēusi kynes tachees katedontai.
sentences.l:
nor your wife, of many gifts; but far from us two, greatly,
beside the ships of the Argives the swift dogs will devour you.”
sentences.i: nor will your wife, she of the many gifts; but very far from the two of us, beside the ships of the Argives, the swift dogs will devour you.”
sentences.n: οὐδ’ ἄλοχος πολύδωρος ‘nor your wife, of many gifts’: the wife is Andromache, and πολύδωρος ‘with many gifts’ is a word whose sense is not fixed, since it can mean the gifts given for her or the dowry she brought. ἄνευθε μέγα ‘far, very far’ and νῶϊν ‘from us two’ is the dual pronoun ‘us two’, Hecuba and Andromache. κατέδονται is the future middle of κατεσθίω ‘devour’, and κύνες ταχέες ‘swift dogs’ the subject. This line closes Hecuba’s speech, and the book goes on to the scene at the gates.
